Any Canadian-listed fund holding US stocks. The fund, a Canadian trust, is the shareholder. It suffers the 15% itself, whatever account you hold its units in. In a taxable account it can pass the credit to you; in an RRSP, TFSA or other registered plan nothing can recover it.
Do not sell early to “reset” the gain. Realizing gains sooner only pays the tax sooner. Deferral is valuable; the gain timing guide shows it.
In a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, do not convert to avoid withholding. It cannot be avoided there. A Canadian-listed fund saves the conversion.

In a taxable account, keep the slips. Claim the foreign tax shown in box 34 of a T3 (or on your broker’s slip) on Form T2209. The credit is limited to the Canadian tax on that foreign income; if your income is very low, part of it may not be usable.

In an RRSP, compare total cost. For a large, long-held US equity position, a US-listed ETF can come out ahead once yield × 15% exceeds the extra yearly fee, and the holding period is long enough to recover the conversion. For small or short holdings the Canadian-listed fund is usually simpler and close in cost.

Judge returns in real, after-tax terms. A fund that shows a 50% gain over 15 years may have made far less in purchasing power. Compare plans in today’s dollars, as the inflation and purchasing-power guide does.

Keep perspective on risk. Equity and balanced funds can fall sharply and recover slowly; no return here is promised. Tax arithmetic matters, but diversification, fees and staying invested matter more.

Keep perspective. Diversification, total fees, your risk capacity and staying invested through market falls matter far more over decades than a fraction of a percent. Returns are uncertain and US stocks can fall sharply in Canadian-dollar terms, through both prices and the exchange rate.

Look at the account first. The account’s tax rules, not the fund, decide whether US withholding can be credited, avoided or not. A fund is not more or less tax-exempt because of the account label on it.

RRSP or RRIF, US-listed securities. Article XXI, paragraph 2 of the treaty exempts dividends and interest received by an arrangement “operated exclusively to administer or provide pension, retirement or employee benefits”. RRSPs and RRIFs are treated as such arrangements, so a US-listed ETF or US share held directly in them normally pays its dividends without withholding.

Separate new pay from an existing holding. Contributing future savings to a TFSA is simple. Moving an existing non-registered fund into a TFSA is a sale for tax purposes, and the inflation part of its gain is taxed then; the in-kind contribution guide explains.

TFSA, FHSA or RESP. These are not retirement trusts for treaty purposes. CRA warns that foreign dividends paid to a TFSA or an FHSA could be subject to foreign withholding tax, and its foreign tax credit folio (¶1.69) says foreign tax on income earned in an RRSP or TFSA does not count for a foreign tax credit. The 15% is simply lost.

Taxable account. US dividends are foreign income, taxed in full at your marginal rate. The US tax withheld is generally credited against the Canadian tax on that income through the federal foreign tax credit, so the withholding is not an extra cost as long as you owe at least that much Canadian tax on it. A Canadian fund passes the foreign income and the foreign tax it paid to you on the T3 slip (boxes 25 and 34), CRA explains, so the credit works through a fund too.

Use the tax-free and tax-deferred room for long-held growth first. The longer you expect to hold, and the higher inflation might be, the more the TFSA’s freedom from tax on both real and inflation gains is worth. The asset location guide discusses what to put where.

A US-listed ETF avoids the withholding only in an RRSP or RRIF, and it needs US dollars. At a conversion cost of 1% each way, converting in and converting back takes about 2% of the money, about $9,607 by year 25 on the larger ending balance. In a TFSA the US-listed ETF pays both the conversion and the withholding, and falls furthest behind, about $33,975.

A capital gain on a fund includes a portion that only restores purchasing power, and in a taxable account that portion is taxed too, because the cost base is not adjusted for inflation. With 4% real growth and 2.5% inflation over 20 years, about a quarter of the reported gain is inflation, and tax takes 19.7% of the real gain instead of the 14.8% headline rate. Interest taxed every year fares far worse. Inside a TFSA neither part is taxed.

A further layer applies when a Canadian-listed fund holds a US-listed ETF that in turn holds stocks outside the US: foreign taxes withheld by those other countries at the bottom level are also lost, and are not shown here.

Canada taxes the capital gain in dollars, not in purchasing power, so the part of a gain that merely keeps up with inflation is taxed like real profit. See how big that part is for a fund held for decades, how it raises the true tax rate on your real return, what September CPI since 2006 implies, and why a TFSA or RRSP changes the arithmetic.

Canada taxes the dollar gain: the proceeds minus the adjusted cost base, as CRA’s capital gains guide defines it, with no allowance for inflation. Half of that gain is included in income. This guide asks how much of the gain is inflation, how much tax falls on it, and what that does to the tax rate on the part of the return that actually made you better off.

In an RRSP holding a US-listed ETF, all of it is reinvested. In an RRSP holding a Canadian-listed fund, or in a TFSA, FHSA or RESP holding either kind, $225 is withheld and never returns, and $1,275 is reinvested. Longer holding helps a little: the deferral of tax until sale lets the untaxed amount compound, and the real part of the gain grows faster than the inflation part when real returns are healthy.

Measure everything in today’s purchasing power. Without tax, the fund would have turned $10,000 into $21,911 of today’s money, a real gain of $11,911. After the tax at sale it is worth $19,568, a real gain of $9,568. Tax took 19.7% of the real gain, not the 14.8% (half of 29.65%) that the headline rate suggests.

None of these figures includes fees. Many Canadian-listed US index funds and their US-listed equivalents differ in management fee by a few hundredths of a percent a year, which over 25 years can be as large as the effects shown. Compare the whole cost, not one line.

Note the distinction. A TFSA or RRSP is an account with tax rules; it does not change the fund’s risk, fees or returns. An RRSP defers tax rather than removing it: withdrawals are fully taxed as income, so it removes the inflation-on-gains problem but taxes the whole withdrawal at your rate at that time.

Other differences sit outside this calculation. A US-listed ETF reports in US dollars and needs records of the exchange rate for each purchase and sale in a taxable account; the currency and cost base guide explains why. Large holdings of US-listed securities can also raise US estate tax questions. Simplicity has value too.

The amounts are smaller than most fund fees, and that is the first lesson. Withholding tax is worth understanding and arranging sensibly; it is rarely worth taking on extra risk, concentration or complexity to avoid.

The answer is not a reason to avoid investing or to fear inflation. It is a reason to understand why the account you hold a fund in matters, and why a low-return investment held in a taxable account can lose purchasing power even when it shows a profit.

The heatmap repeats this for real growth from 1% to 6% and inflation from 0% to 6% over the holding period you enter. With no inflation every cell equals the headline rate. With high inflation and low real growth the effective rate climbs: at 1% real growth and 4% inflation over 20 years, tax takes about half of the real gain. That combination, a cautious investment in a high-inflation period, is exactly when the tax on inflation hurts most.

The last chart follows the same pre-tax return three ways, in today’s dollars. Inside a TFSA nothing is taxed, so the real value grows at the full 4%. In a taxable account with the gain taxed only at sale, the value trails the TFSA by the tax on both parts of the gain. If the same nominal return were paid as interest and taxed in full every year, as GIC interest and much of a bond fund’s distribution are, the real after-tax return falls to about 2.1% a year and tax takes about 57% of the real gain.

The last heatmap scales the withholding loss in a registered account to $100,000 for yields from 0.5% to 4% and holding periods from 5 to 40 years. The withholding drag compounds: it takes 0.225% of the holding every year and the lost amount never grows. Currency conversion for a US-listed ETF is a fixed share of the money moved, paid twice. In an RRSP the US-listed route catches up with the Canadian-listed fund after 10 years. In a TFSA the US-listed route pays both costs.

The withholding takes yield × rate from the holding every year: 1.5% × 15% = 0.225% a year with the defaults. That looks tiny, but money lost early never grows. Against the same stocks with no withholding, which grow to about $482,770 over 25 years at 5% price growth plus 1.5% dividends, a Canadian-listed fund in an RRSP or TFSA ends about $24,862 lower, around 5% of the ending value.

This explains a common rule of thumb: in an RRSP, consider holding the highest-yielding US holdings directly; in a TFSA, which cannot avoid the withholding either way, keep US dividend payers small or hold growth-oriented equities. The asset location guide covers the wider question of what to hold in which account.

This is why the taxable interest guide finds that savings deposits can lose purchasing power after tax, and why balanced funds, which hold bonds, distribute more taxable income each year than equity funds. The income-type guide compares interest, dividends and gains.

To buy what $10,000 bought at the start, you would need about $16,386 at the end. So $6,386, about a quarter of the reported gain, is inflation. The other $19,518 is the real gain, measured in the dollars of the sale year.

US stocks pay dividends after US tax is withheld, and whether you ever get that tax back depends on the account and on how you hold the stocks. US withholding of 15% on dividends is recovered in a taxable account through the foreign tax credit, is avoided by an RRSP or RRIF holding US-listed securities directly, and is lost everywhere else: in a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, and inside any Canadian-listed fund. On a 1.5% yield the loss is about 0.23% a year, a real but modest cost that compounds. Converting currency to avoid it costs money too, so the right choice depends on yield, conversion cost, fees and how long you hold, not on the withholding alone.
